title: Spirals of sunflower, thistle and cone are deformations of helices on a stem

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Spirals of sunflower, thistle and cone are deformations of helices on a stem

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The logarithmic spirals of flat or convex inflorescences and the helices on elongated stems are one phenomenon: the fir-cone, teasel, thistle and sunflower heads are successive geometric deformations of a long, nearly cylindrical stem, on which the same arrangement appears as helices.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the semi-ellipsoidal capitulum of the teasel, the more or less hemispherical one of the thistle, and the flattened but still convex one of the sunflower, are all beautiful and successive deformations of what is typically a long, conical, and all but cylindrical stem.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIV, “On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis”; topic “Helices and logarithmic spirals in phyllotaxis”. Scope: leaf, scale and floret arrangements in plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch14-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.69

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The geometric equivalence can be tested computationally on digitized specimens. Existing data are adequate for examples but likely not for the full developmental assertion spanning all listed plant structures.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map organ positions on 3D surfaces from stems, cones and capitula, geometrically deform each surface to a common cylinder, and test whether the same indexed arrangement becomes helical while surface projections become logarithmic spirals. Topological and parameter continuity supports the claim; discontinuous rearrangement refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Cross-taxon deformation does not itself establish developmental identity.

Open 3D coverage of intact inflorescences is limited.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is that capitulum spirals and stem helices are one arrangement seen on differently shaped surfaces. Sunflower counts and images make the flat case measurable, and a few cone scans represent the elongated case, but the intermediate teasel and thistle forms are not in those files. A geometric mapping can be tried on this uneven sample; it would not yet cover the whole series Thompson lists.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate divergence and parastichy families on elongated cones and on flattened capitula, then apply a geometric compression from cylinder to disc and ask whether one lattice reproduces both. The deformation account is supported if sunflower, thistle, teasel, and cone patterns are the same lattice on different surfaces; it is refuted if their divergence or chirality rules differ in kind rather than by surface shape.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Teasel and thistle heads are not in the sunflower count file, and open cone scans are few species.

A deformation can be drawn between many lattices, so the test needs matched divergence, not a visual resemblance.
